2026 · Research Note 8

Can an algorithm decide which battery electrolyte experiments are worth doing next?

Deep active learning selects lithium-metal electrolyte experiments, then transfers the learned component relationships into larger and modified formulation spaces.

In brief

QuestionCan an algorithm decide which battery electrolyte experiments are worth doing next?
ResultThree active-learning iterations used 128 tested cells and about 4.4% of the stated exhaustive-testing resources; selected formulations enabled roughly three-times longer Li||Li cycling than the reference state-of-the-art electrolytes.
Why it mattersThe model is used to allocate experiments and then reuse learned chemical relationships in new design tasks.
Deep active learning and knowledge transfer for rapid discovery of lithium metal battery electrolytes
Xufeng Hong et al. · Nature Communications · Published 27 March 2026
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-70973-4

The electrochemical problem

Lithium-metal electrolyte performance depends on interactions among salts, solvents, additives, concentrations, and interphases. The resulting formulation space is discrete, noisy, and strongly non-linear, which makes exhaustive testing expensive and simple interpolation unreliable.

The paper asks whether active learning can choose informative experiments, discover high-performing formulations with fewer cells, and then transfer what it learned when the chemical design space changes.

What the researchers did

The first stage combines deep kernel learning with Thompson sampling. The surrogate model estimates performance across a 720-formulation space, while the acquisition strategy selects the next formulations to test by balancing exploration and exploitation.

In the second stage, target statistic coding captures learned component relationships and transfers them to tasks such as a larger 5,400-formulation space and electrolyte problems involving new components or full cells.

What they found

Across the initial random round and three active-learning iterations, the study tested 128 cells. The authors estimate this as 4.4% of the testing resources required for high-confidence exhaustive testing of the original space. After three iterations, selected formulations enabled Li||Li symmetric cells to cycle about three times longer than the state-of-the-art electrolyte references used in the study.

The learned relationships were also transferred beyond the original search space. In the expanded 5,400-formulation space, experimentally tested zero-shot recommendations included formulations with average cycling performance exceeding that achieved after the original iterative search.

Why this matters

Active learning changes the economics of electrochemical discovery because the scarce resource is often not model inference but laboratory measurements. A useful model should therefore reduce the number of experiments needed to reach an informative region of the design space.

The transfer step is equally important. Electrolyte research continually introduces new molecules and constraints; a workflow that must restart from zero each time would lose much of its practical advantage.

One important caution

The reported resource saving is defined relative to a specific exhaustive-testing assumption, and the three-times lifetime result belongs to the selected cell chemistry and test protocol. It should not be read as a universal battery-life multiplier.

Active learning also does not make the underlying electrolyte physics continuous or simple. Recommendations still require experimental validation because formulation–performance relationships remain noisy and system dependent.

Primary source

Xufeng Hong et al. Deep active learning and knowledge transfer for rapid discovery of lithium metal battery electrolytes. Nature Communications (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-70973-4.
